title: The Wheelbarrow
part: PART ONE: TWO WAYS OF KNOWING

pages.text:
*Jun's phone says: 1 bar of signal, 91% battery. Nari's river says: warm and slow.*

The road to the farmhouse was not a road at all. It was a ribbon of packed dirt that wiggled between the corn stubbles and the sweet potato vines. Jun walked in a straight line, his white sneakers striking the dust with precise, rhythmic taps. Nari rolled the wheelbarrow in a zigzag, dodging every root and stone without looking. She hummed a tune that had no name, a steady, low sound that kept her mouth from opening.

Jun did the opposite. He opened his mouth. He pointed at the corn. He held up his phone to the sky. He explained the difference between a corn tassel and a silage plant, citing a video he had watched last Tuesday. He was trying very hard to be interesting. He was also getting very hot, and his round glasses had fogged up.

Nari did not look at him. She looked at the braid over her shoulder. She looked at the mud on the wheelbarrow. She looked at the way Jun kept stepping on the grass, as if he thought the earth would bite him if he looked away. She hummed louder.
pages.image: Nari, a strong sunburnt girl in a faded sunflower-yellow T-shirt with a long black braid, pushes a dented green wheelbarrow down a dusty dirt path while Jun, a thin boy in round black-framed glasses and white sneakers, follows close behind pointing at his phone.

pages.text:
The valley opened up around them, a hundred houses tucked into the green hills like seeds in a pod, while rice paddies stretched out in neat, shiny squares to reflect the bright sky. Corn stalks stood tall and thick, their leaves rustling in a breeze that smelled of wet earth and growing things.

"Red peppers," Nari said, nodding at a row of plants by the fence. "They’re turning color early this year."

"I know," Jun said, tapping his screen. "I saw it on a map. They grow them in this region."

Nari stopped the wheelbarrow. She looked at him, then at the sky, sniffing the air until her nose crinkled slightly as the scent grew heavy with humidity.

"Rain by the end of the week," she said. It was not a question.

Jun checked his weather app. The little sun icon grinned back at him. "The app says ten percent," he said. "Ten percent is almost zero."

Nari snorted, a short, sharp sound like a cat hissing, and pushed the wheelbarrow forward until the wheels crunched over the gravel. "The app doesn’t smell the air," she said. "It doesn’t listen to the cicadas."

The cicadas were screaming. They were so loud the air seemed to vibrate. Jun looked at his phone, then at the sky, and for the first time, he did not know which one to believe.
pages.image: A lush green valley with shiny rice paddies and tall corn stalks, where Nari, a sunburnt girl in a yellow shirt and dark green trousers, stops a wheelbarrow to look at the sky while Jun, a thin boy in glasses and a white T-shirt, holds up his phone.

pages.text:
The farmhouse was low, built of wood and stone, with a wide porch that shaded the door. A pump stood by the wall, its handle worn smooth by years of use. In the yard, straw mats lay out in long rows, and on them, hundreds of red peppers were drying in the sun. They looked like a bright red carpet, waiting for someone to step on it.

Then a door opened.

"Aigoo!"

The sound came from a small, round figure in a bright floral top and a purple sun visor. Halmoni wiped her hands on her apron and rushed down the porch steps. She was small, so small that Jun felt like he was looking at a doll, but her energy was huge.

"Aigoo! My baby! Look at you! Aigoo, you are so thin!"

She did not wait for an answer. She grabbed Jun by the shoulders and hugged him. It was a tight, fierce hug, the kind that squeezed the air out of his lungs. His glasses slipped down his nose and fell off, bouncing onto the dusty ground.

"I can’t see!" Jun squeaked.

Halmoni pulled back, but she did not let go of his arms. She looked at his face, then at his shoes, then at the suitcase in the wheelbarrow. "Aigoo," she said again, but this time, it sounded like worry.
pages.image: A low wooden farmhouse with a wide porch and a yard full of red peppers drying on straw mats, where Halmoni, a small round woman in a bright floral top and purple sun visor, hugs Jun, a thin boy in a white T-shirt, tightly.

pages.text:
Inside, the floor was cool, covered in woven mats. Shoes were left at the door. Jun looked down at his white sneakers. A brown line of mud traced the sole, a dirty border around the clean white rubber. He stepped over the threshold, trying not to drag the dirt further in.

Halmoni was already at the low table. She set out bowls with a clatter. Cold buckwheat noodles in icy broth. Kimchi, bright red and crisp. A bowl of white rice, steaming gently. And in the center, a watermelon the size of a bowling ball, cut into thick red half-moons.

"Eat first," Halmoni said. "Talk later."

Jun reached for his phone. He raised it over the table, framing the noodles, the kimchi, the watermelon. He wanted to show his mother how real this was. He wanted to prove that the village was not just a map.

Nari, who had sat down beside him, rolled her eyes so hard it looked like it hurt. She picked up a chopstick and began to eat, her mouth full, her eyes on the watermelon.

Jun lowered his phone. The noodles looked good. They really did look good. But the photo in his head did not look as good as the real thing. He took a bite. The broth was cold, the noodles chewy, and the taste was something he did not have a name for.
pages.image: A low wooden table with bowls of cold noodles, kimchi, rice, and a watermelon cut into red slices, where Jun, a thin boy in glasses, holds up his phone to photograph the food while Nari, a sunburnt girl in a yellow shirt, rolls her eyes and eats.

pages.text:
The door creaked, and Harabeoji stepped in from the yard. His faded green baseball cap sat low over a face weathered by sun and wind. He wore a striped short-sleeved shirt and tall black rubber boots caked in dark mud.

He did not look at the food. Nor did he look at Jun.

Instead, his gaze swept past the boy to Nari, and finally settled on the woven mat between their legs.

He sat down on the edge of the mat. His posture was rigid. But he did not touch the bowls.

He simply watched them eat. His eyes were dark and steady.

The silence stretched. It was filled only by the sharp clink of chopsticks against ceramic and the high, buzzing hum of cicadas outside the window.

When the last noodle was gone and the bowls lay empty, Harabeoji spoke. His voice was low and dry. It sounded like old leaves skittering across a dusty path.

"Rules of the river," he said. "Vests on. Never alone. Stay with the boat."

Nari nodded without looking up. The rhythm of the words was familiar as a heartbeat. She had known them since she could walk, a part of her as natural as breathing.

Jun reached for his notebook. The pen hovered for a second. Then he began.

He wrote the words down carefully. Then he underlined them twice. He pressed hard enough to make an indent in the paper.

It felt important. Like a promise he had not yet made, but was about to.
pages.image: A dimly lit room with a low wooden table, where Harabeoji, a thin weathered man in a faded green cap and tall black boots, sits silently watching Jun, a thin boy in glasses, write in a notebook while Nari, a sunburnt girl in a yellow shirt, nods.
